rationale: Extensive assessment of the literature across NBIA and Jaberi-Elahi syndrome cohorts demonstrates that basal ganglia iron accumulation is typically absent or undetectable on brain MRI during early infancy and early childhood. Rather than presenting with pathognomonic iron deposition, pediatric presentations are dominated by cerebellar atrophy or pontocerebellar hypoplasia, corpus callosum hypoplasia/dysgenesis, severe developmental delay, hypotonia, and ectodermal features (such as sparse hair). Systematic review of Jaberi-Elahi syndrome cohorts (e.g., Manoochehri et al., 2024) shows that evidence of brain iron accumulation is documented in only a small minority of older evaluated individuals (4 of 28 patients). Mechanistic reviews of NBIA (e.g., Vijeev et al., 2026) corroborate that GTPBP2-related disease belongs to a class of secondary NBIA disorders that occur without early basal ganglia iron deposition. Consequently, brain iron deposition cannot serve as an early clinical or radiological discriminator to distinguish GTPBP2-related disorder from non-iron-accumulating pontocerebellar hypoplasias or early-onset hereditary spastic paraplegias.

evidence.text: Comprehensive literature review of 28 reported Jaberi-Elahi syndrome cases identified brain iron accumulation in only 4 individuals, all of whom presented with iron deposition later in disease progression, while early core features were motor delay (26/28), sparse hair (26/28), speech disorder (24/28), hypotonia (23/28), intellectual disability (23/28), and skeletal abnormalities (23/28).

new_directions.question_text: At what exact median age and on which MRI sequences (e.g., SWI, QSM, T2*) does basal ganglia iron deposition first become quantifiable in GTPBP2 patients?
new_directions.rationale: Clarifying the chronological window when iron accumulation transitions from absent to detectable will help establish age-specific diagnostic algorithms and clarify when SWI/QSM imaging is clinically informative.

new_directions.question_text: Can a combination of sparse hair, cerebellar/corpus callosum hypoplasia, and early hypotonia serve as a validated composite clinical rule to distinguish GTPBP2 from PCH types 1-2 and complex HSPs prior to exome sequencing?
new_directions.rationale: Because iron imaging fails in infancy/childhood, non-radiological discriminating features such as sparse hair combined with pontocerebellar hypoplasia may provide the highest discriminatory power in resource-limited or pre-genetic clinical settings.
